But you can only pick one making the story that she either "hates the woman" or "is her best friend" instead of the simple truth that she is her best friend AND they get into fights as can be explained later by the woman being off of her meds.

If you're someone who doesn't like this type of game, you won't enjoy it so don't buy it. If you do enjoy this type of game, you'll likely be disappointed like I was and won't enjoy it, so don't buy it. Not worth even at a sale.

review_text_raw:
The premise of searching through social media to uncover a hidden group brought me to this game. When I was playing it though the structure of the game felt off to me, there was too little freedom to discover for myself the conspiracy that was going on. Certain necessary options are highlighted beforehand, so that skimming (or even skipping) the text was an option. Any puzzle/detective game that is as on-rails as this one is bound to lack any critical reasoning.

Also the use of Orwellian politics is so reductive that it almost entirely avoids any real political discussion (bad State controls people, we need "freedom", whatever that is).

My advice is that if you want political commentary then read a book instead. If you want a good detective story then read a book instead. Either way I'd rather read a book than play this game any day,

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

I expected to have to do more "detective work", but this is just a choices-don't-make-sense-but-they-matter experience.  Especially in the final chapter, I had little clue what I was supposed to accomplish, and then suddenly I accomplished something and the game was over.

If I could give this a Thumbs-Sideways, I would.  There are a few interesting "scenes" and moments that were surprising, but as it stands, I didn't feel like I was enjoying myself.  Just uploading "datachunks" and waiting for the game to find more datachunks to be uploaded.  Occasionally I had to decide between two conflicting pieces of data, but those choices were less-than-half of the game.  Maybe one-third of the game is "decisions" like that, and the rest is just dragging datachunks from one side of the screen to the other.  Or in some cases, deciding NOT to drag a datachunk from one side of the screen to the other, because it might be misunderstood by your superiors. For example, one comment on a website in-game says "oh no! the torture! ;)" in a playful manner about being bribed with muffins, but if you upload it your boss takes it to mean LITERAL TORTURE and freaks out about it.  So you're told to upload "all the relevant data" but then have no say in how it gets interpreted or used, which impacts upon the relevance of said data.

If you like games that try to make political-statements about things, this is probably up your alley.  I just wanted to solve puzzles, connect clues, etc.  The game highlights all the relevant information, and then connects it to things for you.  Not TERRIBLE, but not what I expected or hoped for. :(

review_text_raw:
I don't review games very often, but I felt that I needed to throw out my two cents on this game. I haven't read any other reviews, so I'm not influenced by what other people think of it.

I went into this game almost entirely blind. I got it a long while ago, and just got around to installing and playing it today. I sat down to give it a quick try, see if I would enjoy it, and ... 3 hours later, I finished the story. It's not a sprawling 100 hour experience, but those 3 hours were intense, and I was locked into the events the entire time.

A brief summary: you play an Investigator using a program called Orwell, which sifts through social media profiles and newspaper articles (and maybe listens in on a few phone calls) to try to track down criminals. Specifically, a bomb has gone off in a public plaza, and you need to find out who did it.

There are some great twists and turns along the way, and I enjoyed myself the entire time. One moment in particular had me literally on the edge of my seat, biting my lip while I listened to a conversation unfold, unable to do anything but wait to see what would happen. This was a conversation that only occurred because of choices that I had made, and in the end, I had to live with the consequences of those choices. It was rough, and it was emotional, but it was amazing.

Anyway, I love this game. I give it a 4/5 on my "arbitrary 5 point rating scale". The writing felt a little clunky at times, which is really the only complaint that I have, and it's not bad enough to really detract from the experience. Please give this game a try!

Graphics: 5/5
 - It's VERY stylized, so it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but I really loved the way everything looked. The UI was clean and easy to maneuver, and the portraits and pictrues were very compelling for me.

Sound: 4.5/5
 - Very immersive music, and the sound effects felt right at home. Since there's no audible dialogue in this game (when you're "listening" to a phone conversation, you're reading the text transcription of that conversation), the music rising and falling gave some amazing feels. There are also times that the music will suddenly move from calm and serene the intense and pounding when you're reading articles or some such, indication that you've found a piece of information that drastically changes things. I give it 4.5 instead of 5 because the different tracks don't flow into each other - when one starts, the previous one stops instantly, giving a weird stutter.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. It takes a little bit more than one hour per episode, maybe faster if you just drag and drop without reading.
Even if having a [i]know it all[/i] tool, there are plenty of mysteries to uncover and discovering bit by bit the personalities and relationships of the people you [strike]spy on[/strike] is pretty addictive.

The presentation is pretty nice with its stylish interface. Graphics isn't the most important part of the game but it's good that it's pleasing to the eyes. The music does also its job, it changes when there's a [b]gasp[/b] moment. 

In summary, I recommend this game if you like simple but well told story in a different way than just watching Netflix. It has a nice conspiracy/detective vibe and getting to the finish is an entertaining (and bumpy) ride.
I have definitely put the season 2 on my wishlist!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A good game in principle but fell short along the way.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Orwell [/h1] is a very interesting game to say the least. While gameplay wise you just have to pull and drag some text into a box, the story is captivating as well as how you influence it.

[b] Gameplay [/b]: So Orwell is a game where you embody Big Brother or more like a part of it, an essential yet very subjective part. You goal will be to choose and extract informations on people from their websites, social medias and other public informations but also the data inside their cellphone, personal computer, private phone calls and message, crossing the border of privacy. You interfere with the story by choosing what information are revelante or not, making you think about which information you want to upload or not to Orwell (the Big Brother server). Futhermore choosing to upload one information can make others being not uploadable because it has some conflict with it (2 piece of information can say opposite thing, it's up to you to choose which one is legit or not). this will makes you even more careful about it, and that's good because even if I just had to pull and drag some text, I really got tense during some phase of the game. Felt very immersive

[b] Art [/b] : The art for the pictures is a tad special, but I liked it a lot. The interface is well done and very comfortable to browse. 

[b] Musics and sounds [/b] : The music really got me in this game, I first expected not bad but plane music for this game but it's really not the case. I think that the music is a big factor of why I got this tense (in a good way) in that not so tense pull and drag gameplay. When something bad happens (or will happen) I felt like I had to do things faster even if this game never had timer or whatsoever like it and that you have all your time.

[b] Story [/b] : The characters that you will dig in their privacy are fairly good, they all have interesting personality and felt really human. Story wise it's a little predictable but, well you ARE the big brother so you had every pieces to know what will happen but what I want to focus on is how you influense the story. In the gameplay part I said that what you want to focus on is wheter a piece of information is revelant or not, but that's not quite true if you don't want to be controlled by big brother, you are a small part of it but an essential one, and indirectly you are the one who control the police and the media in this game, so instead of contribute to big brother you can do the opposite, to give you some ideas. (This game have multiple endings and variations depending of which pieces of information you upload or not)

[b] Summary [/b] :

Pros : 
- The story and mostly how you influence it
- The music
- Fairly good characters 

Cons :
- Maybe a tad short even with the multiple endings but it is a wonderful game so I can't really blame it

90/100 I really enjoyed this game, it's refreshing and really fun and captiving to play. Actually I played a game which is similar to this one before but with puzzle too, the name is Replica and if you played Orwell and liked it you should look into Replica which is a pretty good game (not as good as this one if I recall but well, maybe I am wrong because it has been some times since I last played it, I will look into again and make a review) Still Orwell is not something you should miss, while it is short, I have only found one game that is similar and they are both very good so it's refreshing. If you are bored of your usual AAA games then that's maybe what you need.

Seemingly at random, when you hover over a highlighted piece of information it will not show you the summary of what gets uploaded to Orwell. This is a huge bummer because then you are uploading information that you may think one thing but the game thinks another. Sometimes logging out and going to the main menu fixes it, but not always.

I went back and played through it a second time to see different outcomes and to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed my time with the game and would recommend it on sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Worth it? Yes. DLC? Yes. Get it on sale? Probably, but it's worth the price if you have disposable income.
I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. 

-There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need.

-This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright.

-Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

My first contact with Orwell was back in 2017 when there was some event in my local town square where there were couple of PCs with few games on it for everyone interested to play, and Orwell was one of them. This game actually taught me very very advanced English and I shall ever be so grateful for it.

This game is based on George Orwell's novel "1984" where he mentions the phrase "Big Brother" for the first time. I've never read it but after playing both games [yes there is a second one] I think I just might. Basically it means that you're being spied on all the time. I could describe and explain what "ORWELL" really stands for but that would be a huge spoiler and nobody wants that, right? It is very political, but if I got to play it, a person who knows jack crap about politics, everyone can play it.
If you've never played it before, the average play time is around 4-5 hours, but once you get to do more playthroughs in it can be done in little over 2 hours. I also really liked the low-poly design of the pictures, it really adds to the overall graphics experience.

What was a bad move in my opinion was the fact that you're not actually doing any research on your own, the game automatically highlights the important "datachunks" for you to upload to a corresponding profile. But on the other hand I can imagine how difficult it would have to be for the developers to implement this function. If everyone would put there even just slightly different things it would be a mess. But it's a nice thought to think about.

If you're interested in politics or simply want to improve your English, play this game. I'm pretty sure you will have to translate every third word or so because like I said, it is very professionally written but that's the beauty of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard. What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience. Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B. One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold. So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.

review_text_raw: An interesting take on a mass surveilance video game, where you actually get to act a bit like a Big Brother esque detective. While the puzzle aspect is enjoyable, certain mechanics do result in feelings of repetitiveness and a lack of free exploration. More choices and information opportunities could be interesting, as well as perhaps a bit of tampering with the UI (everytime I use the Listener it feels like I have to wait two minutes for the computers to stop talking to each other just to click the datachunk, as it keeps moving down the page). Overall though, and especially as there have only been two episodes released, I have enjoyed this game enough to play each installment twice through, with different results, and still want to continue exploring the world Orwell allows us to explore: one of deceit, fear, and an underbelly of self-consiousness as you realize that you Big Brother.

review_text_raw:
[h1] ORWELL REVIEW [/h1]


[b] What is Orwell? [/b] 
Orwell is a story-driven puzzle/mystery game in which you, someone outside 'The Nation', take control of Orwell - the latest security system designed to counteract terrorism, etc. Its a game that focuses more on giving you an experience with its story and plot rather than with engaging gameplay. 

[u] STORY [/u] 
Orwell isn't shy in showing its influences from George Orwells '1984' (clearly), and thats a good thing. '1984' is considered by many to be one of the best pieces of literature ever written, and with very good reason - it predicts a horrible shift in society which results in a dystopian state run with an iron fist and constant survelliance and information control on its populace. George Orwell's novel takes place after this dytopian rule has been established for years, so we do not truly understand how it became so all-powerful to begin with, however, Orwell takes a look at what it may be like at the start of this rule, with a brand new system, called ORWELL, being used to solve a terror attack on 'The Nation'. When Orwell wrote '1984' there was no internet, or social media, etc. and this game takes a look at how '1984' would be had those things been considered, and trying to basically update '1984' for a modern audience and make it culturally relevant today is no small feat, and happily, I can say they have done a superb job of capturing, while updating, George Orwell's original vision.  

Overall Story Score = 9/10 (Masterful) 


[u] GAMEPLAY [/u]
Gameplay in Orwell is probably the games weakest point as there's not much actual 'gameplay' involved. For the most part Orwell's gameplay consists of reading text documents, web pages, phonecall logs, emails, etc. and finding relevant text and info and attaching it to certain peoples files. While this may sound completely mundane it is actually quite a refreshing take on detective gameplay and feels like you are genuinely investigating people. Although, personally, towards the climax of the game I found trying to find that one last clue to tie things together quite frustrating and slowed the pace of the game. 

Overall Gameplay Score = 6/10 (Good)


[u] GRAPHICS [/u] 
Orwell uses a rather unique cell-shaded polygon art style, very similar to something you would find in a visual novel, and it compliments the game well. As someone who isnt a huge fan of completely drawn art styles Ifound myself really liking the approach this game took in its art direction. 

Overall Graphics Score = 7/10 (Great) 


[u] SOUND [/u] 
Orwell has a nice relaxing soundtrack for the most part with occasional moments of high intensity. The soundtrack perfectly fits the game and was particularly noticable during certain parts of the game which greatly increased the impact of those moments. Also, the soundtrack doesn't get annoying or repetative at any point which is impressive considering the length of time you are listening to it. Saying all that though, its by no means a memorable soundtrack or anything special. 

Overall Sound Score = 6/10 (Good) 


[u] LASTING APPEAL [/u] 
It took me roughly 4 hours to play through the story once, and I am plannign at some point to play through it once more, but that will probably be the max I play. I personally wouldn't pay full price just purely due to the price-to-playtime ratio but on sale I would definitely pick it up. Overall though the lasting appeal is quite poor due to it being a story driven game all based on a whodunnit payoff, which makes replayability a bit less appealing. There are multiple endings however so if you want to get all of them you may get more out of it than most.

Overall Lasting Appeal Score = 4/10 (Below Average)


[b] OVERALL SCORE = 7/10 - Great [/b]

review_text_raw:
The game that lets you be the judge, jury, and perhaps executioner.  How do you feel about big brother?

Orwell is an excellent puzzle/detective-type game which has you working for a national surveillance test, poring over news articles, social media, phone calls, emails, text messages, you know it!

The setup is very straightforward, who is the terrorist responsible?  Finding out will require a lot of reading of materials, sometimes many times, as you select "data chunks" to give to the Orwell program for analysis (and potentially new materials to look over!)  In that way the play is quite simple, just drag and drop highlighted data, but be careful!  Not all data is current, and some data conflicts!  You also need to take into account the personalities of the people you are investigating, are they hiding something? Are they boastful?  Be aware that in many ways, you will reap what you sow.

The game is pretty simple to play, in my opinion, and you are basically being hand-held over the first in-game day.  The challenge comes from the narrative you want to put into Orwell, will you seek out the truth or serve the state?  Something that was very unexpected for me was the emotional response to events in the game.  At one point I actually cried: I prevented a catastrophe, saving lives, which felt very good, but it laid bare the potential effectiveness of a system that seeks to remove all privacy and could have went wrong very easily.

I also want to say something to the more pessimistic or paranoid about games where you serve something 'evil' and close to reality: this is a story-puzzle game, and has a very defined message.  A CIA AI tutor it is not.

I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good mystery and most especially likes to read.  I wish there were more games where you teeter on the edge of being a web junkie and a librarian, ha!

review_text_raw: Linear puzzles with drag-and-drop solutions. Can't advance even when the next suspect or clue is blatantly obvious because you have to go back and find something really silly, like favorite food, in order to then find the name of a suspected terrorist (which you can easily figure out, without the goddamned cupcake information). Buy The Black Watchmen instead.
